To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the inflammatory process is central to the pathogenesis of demyelination in MS, that the inflammatory process in MS culminates in the interaction between microglia, oligodendroglia and myelin and that these interactions are regulated by a complex network of cytokines, chemokines and growth factors.

(a) the inflammatory process in the brain depends on the availability of lymphocytes in the blood and their ability to migrate into the brain, (b) the inflammatory process culminates in contact between microglias and oligodendroglial-myelin units and (c) the failure of precursor glial cells to enter demyelinated regions is due to the failure to provide the appropriate growth factor environment.

(i) inflammatory processes in the nervous system are initiated in the blood vessels, (ii) these processes are dependent upon the availability of circulating activated lymphocytes, (iii) these processes can be influenced by treatments which limit the availability of lymphocytes or their migration into the nervous system, (iv) inflammatory processes in multiple sclerosis culminate in contact with microglia and oligodendroglia which are damaged by local release by microglia of the cytokine tumour necrosis alpha
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the mechanisms which underlie the inflammatory process in multiple sclerosis, the mechanisms which underpin the failure of remyelination, and how these processes might be influenced by treatment.

the cellular and molecular basis of inflammatory and remyelination processes in the central nervous system, with the aim of identifying new therapeutic targets in multiple sclerosis and related disorders.
the cellular mechanisms which underlie inflammatory brain disease and the potential for repair of the damaged nervous system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
multiple sclerosis is a disease of the immune system which is expressed by inflammation of the brain, but that this is only a part of the disease process.
the inflammatory process is a key component in demyelinating disease and that the treatment of these diseases should be based upon the reduction or prevention of inflammation.
there is a strong case for a combined therapeutic approach to repair demyelineation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inflammatory process in multiple sclerosis is not the only factor which determines disability.
the brain is not a closed system and that the inflammatory response is not an uncontrolled event.
we have shown that inflammatory processes can be limited in the nervous system and that this can be associated with a reduction in lesion size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a lot more that can be done to repair demyelinative lesions in multiple sclerosis.
there is a window of opportunity in which to repair the lesions in the human nervous system.
the immune system is not the only player in the field.
